On the Orders of the Day:

I should like to call the attention of the government to the fact that several weeks ago I brought the matter of the diversion of water for the Chicago drainage canal before the House on a motion which was debated, and at the request of the government, the debate was adjourned. On my motion an order was made for the production of papers on [DOT]the subject, and later certain papers were tabled. In the meantime great damage is being done to navigation on the Great Lakes, and in several harbours the depth of water is from one to two and three feet lower than last year. What is being done, or what will be done about this matter? Several deputations from Ontario have gone to Washington in relation to the question, although they have done nothing and do not represent Canada. If the League of Nations is such a success, why not let them take a hand in this and also in the matter of the Toronto viaduct? If the government can get nowhere on this subject, when will an opportunity be afforded to again discuss the matter? Furthermore will the government do something?-as I do not wish to occupy further time with it this session.

The Prime Minister's
answer does not seem adequate, and I feel, as well, that the House is entitled to a fuller statement as to the present situation of the controversy. Can the Prime Minister not give the House some information as to what, if any, progress is being made towards curing what is fast becoming an intolerable situation in the condition created by the Chicago drainage canal?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the application is asking
to transfer 10,000 cubic feet of water to be used, and objection is being taken to this and the controversy is now proceeding before the Senate committee at the present moment, as well as an action in the court which presumably will be heard this fall. That is the situation at the moment. A protest from this government has been lodged, Mr. Stewart, on behalf of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, has been present at the hearing, although taking no official part in it.

My point is this: The
hearing before the Senate committee is in effect the hearing of an application for a further diversion, really, no doubt, a confirmation of the present unauthorized diversion up to 10,000 cubic feet per second. Is the government's attitude at the present time merely being represented before the Senate committee? If that is the attitude, I consider it not only inadequate but not dignified, as respects what the government should do under the circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved:
The third reading of Bill No. 46, respecting the construction of a Canadian National Railway line from Lloydminster, in the province of Saskatchewan, northwesterly 45 miles.

subtopic: BILLS PROPOSED TO AUTHORIZE THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext:
I
am very much in favour of this bill going through, but I wish to take this opportunity to refer to a statement that was made in this House when the bill was read a second time. The proposed railway will be built from Lloydminster in a northwesterly direction. The Canadian Pacific Railway, to-day have a line that is built from the east as far as the Battle river, some twenty miles south of the town of Lloydminster. It is their intention I understand to eventually go to Vegreville. The shortest way to Vegre-ville would be to go west of where they are, instead of going to Lloydminster and then back northwest and then to Vegreville. If it goes to Lloydminster it means we will have a duplication of railways running northwest from that town. When this was brought up previously in this House, I recommended that we should do all we could to encourage the Canadian Pacific to build westward and so serve a very large country in need of a railway instead of going north to Lloydminister. It is not that I do not wish Lloydminster to have a railway; it will be very well supplied when the Canadian National builds its extra line in there. But when the discussion was taking place in the House, the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McConica), in referring to that part of my constituency

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
through which I suggested that the Canadian Pacific should build, referred to it as "not a very good country." Later on in the Railway committee, he informed the members that the country was no good and that there were no people there. This information has gone abroad, and I might say that it is very much resented by the people of that section of country which is very badly in need of railway facilities. I think anything that is said in this House that would have a tendency to stop, any railways, public or private, from going in there, is doing a great deal of harm.

I observe that
we have as the winding up item "agricultural implements on hand, April 10, 1924." I take it that that must be a refund. Does my hon. friend propose to submit to the House a vote for that refund, or how is the money to be paid? I should have thought that a vote would be necessary, but I want to hear from the minister himself on the matter.

The matter is dealt with in the act and will have to pass through the Treasury Board. If this is only an estimate we cannot submit a vote. However, I will consider this feature of the subject, and I am glad my hon. friend has directed my attention to it.

The statement
of the minister that the amount is only an estimate, is not to the point, for every single amount voted here is but an estimate. But a sufficient sum of money is provided in supply to meet these estimates. There ii no doubt that a liability is created by statute; but in connection with a matter of this kind,
which arises not by reason of the administration of the tax-which would give some right to the board to take action under the Audit Act-but arises as a matter of new legislation of this House, there should be a vote contained in the supplementaries to justify the payment.

My hon. friend is on sound
ground and I say again, I am glad he has directed my attention to this aspect of the matter.

With regard to
"materials consumed in process of manufacture," what business is contemplated? We have information as to the other lines, because we have the customs items given against each one of them; but we have no information which would enable us to check this one. It is on page 3 of the list, just above the large item.

This is a widespread item, as
my hon. friend can see.

Before the minister answers my question, can he tell us how these amounts are arrived at? Are they deductions from last year's figures, and if they are, are they deductions from those amounts which have actually been collected, or from those which ought to have been collected?
They are based on importations, and records of production in Canada, minus export.

Then they are
not based on actual collections?
No.

They are based on what ought to have been collected. Now, yesterday my hon. friend told me that, of the 3,170 companies which were in arrears, fifty per cent were in arrears previous to the assumption of office by his government. That would mean that they were in arrears under the legislation of 1920 or at least under that of 1921. Has the minister any definite particulars now in regard to that?

I have no further particulars
than those I gave yesterday.

Has my hon.
friend been able to get them?
No.

I pointed out
before that this answer which I have already quoted, and which was supposed to be in reply to a charge mad.e that taxes were not collected, instead of answering that charge only emphasizes the gravamen of it; it shows

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
inordinate delays in collecting taxes which ought to be concurrent taxes. Surely my hon. friend should be able to give us a little definite information in regard to what is a matter of very grave moment. He must see that instead of helping the situation he only aggravates it, when he alleges that fifty per cent of these delinquent corporations or individuals, have been owing taxes as far back as 1920, or at any rate 1921. The thing is assuming absurd proportions, if we are supposed to collect these taxes fairly and honestly, without fear, favour or affection. My hon. friend simply confesses an unreasonable delay on the part of the department, and it seems to me that in justice to his own government he ought to give us some satisfactory explanation. If such explanation is not forthcoming I must tell the minister that in my view it will be the duty of parliament to consider a motion for the appointment of a committee to investigate the matter of the sales tax.

As I pointed out to my hon. friend yesterday, in regard to some of these cases provision is made in the act for appeals, and some of the companies have appealed; some have got into the courts. Other companies, again, have failed. When, however, you take into consideration the total collections already made I think my hon. friend will agree that the arrears are not so very great, after all. I am free to say that in my opinion my hon. friend's criticism may do some good, and I agree with him that as far as possible the taxes should be collected without undue delay, so long as no unnecessary hardship or injury accrues to any firm.

Will the minister not go a little further and agree with me that the House ought to know whether or not there are, in connection with the sales tax, arrears which have been allowed to remain in abeyance ever since his government came into office? And that is not an allegation on my part; it is the statement we have had from the minister, for we have been told that about half of them were of that character. Surely my hon. friend will admit that this information should be given to the House when we are considering the efficiency of this legislation and the manner in which it is being forced.

I will direct these observations to the attention of my colleague so that when he later on brings down some legislation touching the matter he may be prepared to give a statement as to the real amounts that are probably tied up in the courts and as to Wir Henry Drayton.]
the number of firms that have failed. There are some details which I admit my hon. friend is entitled to.

I have already shown, from the information that has been given me, that 442 cases were delayed owing to the firms and individuals being in liquidation, while 431 are retail bakers and confectioners who are awaiting the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Rex vs. Versailles Sweets. But has not that decision been given?
I cannot say:
Surely the expert would know whether that decision has been given or not.
My hon. friend will realize that the administration of the act is not in my department.

It is a pity that my genial friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) has not been here to give us a little light on the subject. But it is not my fault that he is absent, and perhaps my hon, friend will get some one from the department to tell him how the matter stands.
I will ask the department tc have a statement prepared for my hon. friend, and, if it is desired, that statement can be tabled.	.

The minister, I think,
should consider some better method of imposition and security in regard to these taxes. It is somewhat incongruous and undignified that the Dominion of Canada in respect of taxes should be pottering away with four hundre'd or five hundred bankrupt concerns, seeking to collect its toll, or awaiting the time when perhaps these concerns will be able to pay. There may be an odd instance of oversight, or delay, or mistake, or something of that kind, which could be justified; but to have such a general situation as this in regard to hundreds of concerns, in one class of cases, and even thousands in others, is altogether unjustifiable. It is not right that the Dominion of Canada should be standing creditor in this matter, hoping some day to get something. We should not have a tax that necessarily puts us in that position. What I am trying to impress on the minister is this: If we have a tax of such a magnitude that it virtually becomes a tax on capital and therefore not payable in cash, then it ought to be brought to the level where it can be payable in cash. And it is not equitable that a great many people should have to pay the tax

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
immediately while thousands of others should have the tax tossed about on the waves until at last they are engulfed. I think the minister has his tax now at a level where it is virtually a capital levy, because if profits are not made you cannot pay the tax, and that is why the minister finds himself with three thousand odd accounts outstanding. The sales tax should! be at a level where it in no case can become a capital levy, and there should be sucl) methods of collection and security that he would not be standing by with other creditors waiting for "something to turn up."

May I say in justice to the
department and the minister (Mr. Bureau) who is absent that this statement appears in the return brought down on May 7, which will be found at page 1834 of Hansard:
Of the 2,466 firms and individuals in arrears of sales tax for a period of over three months, 431 are retail bakers and confectioners who have refused to pay sales tax pending the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Rex vs. Versailles Sweets; 442 are cases of firms and individuals in liquidation; 363 firms and individuals are paying arrears by instalments and prosecutions have been entered in 463 cases.
So I think my right hon. friend will admit that the department is following up the matter fairly well.

Very well; what is the
situation? There are some four hundred out of three thousand that claim at least a rightful delinquency; there is a precedent in litigation that they are waiting. Of the balance, about four hundred are in liquidation, with the minister standing by hoping to get his share; and there are some four hundred more in litigation. Altogether I figure, as the minister read the statement, fourteen hundred of fifteen hundred are accounted for in this way, and with regard to the balance there is nothing doing at all. But my point is this: When the minister has a tax which lands him in that position there is something wrong. The minister should not have three thousand cases outstanding in the collection of any tax. Either there is delinquency in the government or there is unsoundness in the tax, one or the other. I am disposed to think there is both, but in all charity to the administration I fancy that the latter is the main cause. A tax on the present scale is unsound and becomes in many cases a capital levy. This is what I want to press home on the minister. There may be delinquency too, I would be rather surprised if there is not. But though there are all these cases outstanding, it does not necessarily follow I
think the main reason for the difficulty of collection is that the tax is on such a scale that it is fundamentally unsound, because the minister should not be in the position of a creditor standing by in three thousand cases of arrears.

It is fair also to the department that, referring to the observations of my right hon. friend, I should give the remainder of the statement brought down on May 7, a portion of which I have already quoted. It continues as follows:
In the balance of the cases the department is corresponding with the firms and individuals concerned with a view to making satisfactory arrangements for payment of arrears before legal action is taken.
These latter cases require nursing as drastic action would probably result in financial failures.
4. In default of satisfactory arrangements for payment of arrears legal action is taken.
I think it is fair to the department to say that they are following up the outstanding cases very well. When one stops to consider the thousands of collections that they are making throughout Canada, I think this condition of affairs will compare fairly well with the collections in any large wholesale business whose operations extend all over the Dominion.

Maybe so; but does the minister suggest that the government should, in respect of its tax collections, be in a position corresponding to that of a wholesale merchant doing business for profit? Not at all. That is What I am trying to drive home. He says the Minister of Customs is corresponding with some thousands of people in arrears, and that in several cases he is getting payment by instalments-I suppose so much a week.
No, longer than that.

Well, a month-I would say, more likely ten years. In other cases he is wet-nursing the situation. All this is not right. No tax should put us in that position. Either the tax is wrong or the collection is wrong. The minister himself, I think, must admit that. I appeal to the new leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Mc-Master). Does he think the government of Canada should, in respect of three thousand cases of tax arrears, be in the position of nursing the accounts and getting payments per week, per month or per year? Is that situation in itself justifiable on any conceivable ground? It cannot be. Does he not think that it is accounted for by one of two things-and more probably by the first I shall name-by the fundamental unsound-

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
ness of the tax as at present imposed and the scale upon which it is imposed, or the securities taken therefor; or, secondly, by delinquency in collection?

The leader of the
opposition has appealed to me in a borrowed name. In reply, I would say to the committee that if there are a number of delinquent accounts I think it is better in the interests of the country and, in the long run, in the interests of the treasury, that these should be nursed along in order that the largest possible amount may be collected, and in order that firms should not be driven to the wall. I think that is reasonable common sense. I would trust that the charity of which the hon. gentleman has spoken would cover any failure of the government in pushing the thing to the extremity which, apparently, he would like.

Mr. Chairman, may I point out to my right hon. friend that the tax system he is criticising came into force on January 1, this year? Now, in the statement tabled the total arrears of three months and under numbered only 704. So he cannot attribute the condition to the unsoundness of the act.

I was going to point out another aspect of the matter, but first I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) on his very ready acceptance of the new title which the leader of the opposition gave to him.
I disclaimed it. There is another instance of Tory unfairness!

In listening to these
delinquent tax cases one's recollection is naturally thrown back to the old election cry with regard to the Riordon case. The House in Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Gordon in the Chair.
Resolved that it is expedient to amend the provisions of The Income War Tax Act, 1917, and amending acts and to provide:-

Mr. SPEAIvMAN:	In cases where the
income tax which was due in April had already been paid on the basis of a $300 exemption, is there a refund, or to what date does this apply?
I understand that the officers of the department have accepted some returns on the basis of $500 exemption, and I imagine that it is the intention to make remission.

This is a very proper
exemption, but it does not go far enough. It is unfortunate that there should be two rival income taxes, Dominion, and municipal at similar times collected in cities. For example, in Toronto bills were sent out for the municipal income tax on the 18th May, and you have to pay the whole tax in one instalment. Then there is a double-header by the Dominion, payable on 1st May, or in instalments. Both the province and the Dominion cannot be right as to the validity of this tax. The province claims the right to impose an amusement tax-a war tax-in the province; the city has an income tax; and the Dominion comes along and imposes an income tax under what it calls the Income War Tax Act, 1917, under "Militia and Defence", section 91 of the British North America Act. These income taxes by the Dominion, provincial and municipal authorities ought to be co-ordinated, because this is unfair and unjust to small wage-earners in the larger centres of population. No income tax at all should be imposed on those receiving an income under $5,000.
I am glad the minister has seen fit to grant some exemption under section 1, but in England to-day they have marked down the

Ways and Means-Income Tax
income tax by fully 50 per cent, and1 the smaller wage-earners under $5,000 are being given the benefit of that. Under the Mellon bill in the United States, small wage-earners under a certain income of $5,000 have a total exemption. With the high cost of living in the big cities, the working classes, school teachers and other small wage-earners are asking that they be exempted from the provisions of this so-called federal Income War Tax Act, as they have enough municipal taxes to pay.
The war has been over for nearly six years, and when this income tax was first imposed, it was thought that it would last only for the period of the war but it seems a fixture. A man receiving a fixed income of five or six thousand dollars has to bear the big burden of ddbt in this country. He is taxed to death, His rent has not been diminished. His breakfast table, food, coal, and so on-prices are going up and almost nothing coming down. A man cannot even go to a moving picture show without having to pay a double header provincial amusement tax under what the province calls a "war tax". I claim that this provincial tax is ultra vires of the provincial legislature under the system of taxation imposed under the British North America Act under the heading of "Militia and Defence," which is exclusively assigned to the Dominion. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), last session, when this matter was up, said, that he was going to look into the validity of this provincial amusement tax. The municipalities are asking the government to relieve them of this war income tax. The municipalities' methods of raising taxation are very limited, whereas this legislature has unlimited methods of taxation. The municipalities are finding it very hajrd to get along with the large number of Dominion and provincial burdens imposed upon them, and I think the income tax field might have been left as it was in pre-war days entirely as a tax for the municipalities, without having the provinces come along and encroach on this ground which the municipalities have had since confederation, and without having the Dominion too, come along and invade that field which should be left entirely to the municipal field. The municipalities have certain rights and municipal conventions throughout Canada. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) used to be at the head of one of these associations of municipalities, namely that for his province. These organizations are protesting as to the validity, the necessity and the form of this double income tax. The municipalities of Canada
paid a large part of the war debt. In the city from which I come $14,000,000 of purely Dominion burdens were assumed on account of the war, in insurance grants, to recruiting, Red Cross, Patriotic fund and in many other forms of war burdens which this legislature would otherwise have had to pay for. There should now be some relief for the municipalities, six years after the end of the war, from this intolerable burden. I represent an industrial city, a city in which the working classes are clamouring for the elimination of this unjust income tax. It is very doubtful whether, as a matter of policy, it should ever have been enacted. Surely, the department is now going to adopt the policy of the present Minister of Finance when last session he said that he was going to look into the method of taxation of the provinces, and see whether some of the burden imposed by them could not be eliminated in view of their receiving a federal subsidy to maintain provincial institutions.
I also wish to protest against the method of collecting this tax. Almost the same day and the same month are selected for the collection of this tax as are selected by the municipality, and surely there should be some simpler form of return and method of collecting the tax. A man would have to be a Philadelphia lawyer to figure out what his assessable income is with the exemptions and qualifications and the huge four-page form to be made in triplicate. He gets no proper notice of the tax; has to make up his own bill, and if wrong he is hailed to court and asked to pay a tax which, probably, he does not understand and for which he may be paying on a bill overcharged. However good a mathematician a man may be I am sure he must experience at least some difficulty, or at any rate annoyance, in making out the returns. Speaking for myself, I can frankly say that it is only at the cost of a considerable effort that I am able to get my own returns in in time. I have never been in default in this respect, but it is only by taking the greatest pains and at the expense of a good deal of time that I can get the thing done-and I used to be a fair mathematician. It is a complicated business making out returns for the municipality, the province and the Dominion, and I think that it would be well to have some simpler form on which a man could state in three or four lines just what his income was. At present it is necessary to fill out in triplicate a statement covering four pages and the average man who is willing to pay his tax objects strenuously to this lengthy form.

Ways and Means-Income Tax
Before I conclude I want to urge the government during the coming recess to provide an exemption for all those who are in receipt of an income of less than $6,000. At the present time the men of small fixed income, who can least bear the burden, are taxed to death. The tax collector has no trouble in getting after these $6,600 people; they are more readily got at than war profiteers, the jobbers, or the profiteers of the present day. The city assessor, in the case of these other people, has his work cut out, but it is the small man who gets hit the hardest; in fact, the small men pays the bulk of the taxes, both municipal and federal. I should say that the city and the town people who are receiving modest incomes pay 95 per cent of these income taxes, and this form of taxation is unfair, unjust and inequitable. Futhermore, it does not apply uniformly to the various provinces of the Dominion, for certain classes of citizens do not pay anything. I am not moved by any desire to raise captious objections when I bring this matter to the attention of the committee; I have been asked by many public bodies, including ratepayers' associations and other organizations, to state the case. The tax collector, I emphasise, gets the small man at every turn; be gets him at the breakfast table, he gets him when he buys his coal; and in regard to rent, clothing and everything else the wage-earner and the man with the small income are made the scapegoat. The small man hardly comes into the house without discovering that the municipal assessor has increased his assessment some $300 or $400. I would suggest to the government that the time has come when it should abandon the municipal field of taxation altogether which it has encroached upon now for eight or nine years. The Dominion government should realize that the municipalities assumed burdens during the war and contributed to various patriotic charities such as the Red Cross and the Patriotic fund, besides doing their share sn regard to the Victory loans; and having done that I think they are entitled to some generous reciprocal treatment on the part of the federal government, and the government might leave the income field to them as in the years prior to the war. I do not say for a moment that people should object to paying any taxes that are due in relation to the war, because every one wants to meet his share of the war obligations of this country, and gladly does so. But I do think that the Dominion government has invaded the municipal field too long and should now abandon it; I would say that they might do this after 
this year. I do not see why they could not find some other method of raising the money now obtained through taxation of the small income men; they should tax other people than the wage-earner and the man who gets less than $6,000. There are those on the higher scale of life who could better afford to pay taxation than these people. In the United States the people are refusing to tolerate a similar state of affairs any longer and the state legislatures have presented a petition to Washington, with the result that the Mellon bill is brought down to afford some relief in this income tax respect. This is one of the most unpopular forms of taxation to-day, because the bulk of this tax, which last year amounted to $72,000,000, is paid by the industrial classes of the cities and towns and mainly by the small wage-earners, already over taxed and imposed upon in double header and repeater forms of duplicate taxes. There are those who give in their income at, say, $10,000; but it is difficult for the tax collector to ascertain how much they really do get, because at the end of the year their earnings amount to a great deal more than this and they vote themselves $50,000 and put it in as a bonus and not an income; I repeat, in closing, that the government ought to abolish this form of income taxation or at least to exempt the man who gets less than $6,000, because this form of taxation is quite unpopular and at present it is not equitable and further the government should abandon the municipal field and leave as formerly the income tax form to the municipalities and Check up the illegal amusement taxes of the provinces or deduct from their subsidy the over collections not their due, as the amusement tax is illegal.

Whether my few remarks
will be strictly relevant to the clause under discussion I do not know, but I presume there will be no objection to my brief statement at this stage. Under the present federal income tax law where a married man is living under conditions of such freedom from dependents as allows him an exemption of only $2,000 he is immediately penalized if his wife is taken away by death and his exemption is decreased to $1,000; and conversely if a married woman is enjoying an exemption of $2,000 she is similarly penalized if the husband dies. It has been represented to me in several quarters that therein this is probably an injustice to such widower or widow, and I *wish to submit the matter respectfully to the hearing of the committee. In Ontario in connection with municipal income taxation there is no such law; that is to say, if the

householder enjoys an exemption of $2,000 that exemption stands independently of the visit of death to his or her marital partner; and even during the last session of the Ontario legislature two private bills were introduced, the purpose of one being to increase the exemption to $2,500 and the other to increase it to $3,000 in the case of all householders. I admit that in neither of these cases was the bill passed, but those circumstances are not unindicative of public opinion in that province in regard to this matter. The object of that phase of the Ontario law, or certainly the tendency thereof, is to make for the upbuilding and maintaining of the home. The Ontario law recognizes the householder, who is assessed as such, and as to the term employed in the Ontario Act: "Householder and assessed as such," I do not believe there is any substantial ambiguity. It also recognizes, or at least it is interpreted as recognizing, the head of the family, who gets an exemption of $2,000, whether he is a householder or not. It does occur to me that the keeping together of the home is an important factor in the success of our Canadian citizenship, the household or the home being peculiarly the unit of the Canadian nation. I submit to the consideration of the minister therefore the facts and considerations which I have so feebly advocated.

I go further
than my hon. friend in connection with this subject which I am glad he has brought to the attention of the committee. It seems to me that there is an absolute anomaly here and I do not know whether any steps have been taken so far to remedjr it. I frankly tell my hon. friend that it was mv intention to take steps in this direction. has died. The married woman of yesterday becomes the widow of to-day. She may have a little income, but the support and sustenance which she got from her husband are gone. But under the British North America Act the federal government is supreme and has the right to impose whatever taxes in the judgment of parliament are deemed to be in the best interests of the country. By the same act the right of the provinces is limited to the levying of direct taxation. My hon. friend also thought we should have a uniform date for collection of taxes. We have at present a uniform date for the collection of federal taxes. My proposal is that the incomes received by the husband and wife from whatever source or sources shall for taxation purposes be considered as joint income and shall be taxed as such.

Now I propose to tell you
why. I expected opposition from that quarter, but I submit that the proposal is eminently fair. Let us take the situation of the farmer; it is the one I am best acquainted with. The farmer and his wife work together, and the wife works judt as hard as the farmer does.

I know that if the farmer's wife has an income from some other source it is considered separately and is not taxed unless it exceeds $2,000. But a man in any other walk of life may have a taxable income; his wife may have a large income, and both receive the exemption because they are married. Let me give an illustration that came to my notice and that will bring home to you the point I have in mind. This was placed before me, I may say, by the inspector of taxation in the city of Winnipeg. An unmarried man was a clerk in a certain establishment, getting $2,500 a year. I should like to say a word in support of the views expressed by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). It does seem to me that the incomes of husband and wife in most normal cases constitute one income, and that it is unfair to divide that income into two whether it is derived from husband or wife and to grant exemptions in regard to both. It is particularly unfair in the province of Quebec because we have two systems there. One is the system of community of property-where the husband is supposed to own everything, where all the income belongs to him-and the system of separation as to property where the wife can enjoy her separate income, as she does in the English speaking provinces. It means this:	A man may have an income of
$10,000 and if he is married and has community of property with his wife he gets the exemption only on an income of $2,000. There would be an exemption of $2,000 on an- income of say, $10,000. That would leave $8,000 to be taxed. But let us suppose that the man has married under the form of separation as to property.

In the case of community of property, the two incomes being joined, the income tax might be very much greater because the super tax and surtax might be very material. Thus community of property might increase the income tax.
Exactly.
And the separation of property on the other hand might mean a decreased income tax.
That is the point I am trying to make.
That point should be made quite clear.

I will endeavour to
make it still clearer. Under the regime of community as to property the husband is regarded as the sole recipient of income. His income, let us say it is $10,000, will be subject to one exemption of about $2,000, and the taxable portion will be $8,000. Let us suppose another man is married under the regime
of separation as to property and he has the right, under his marriage contract, to donate certain property to his wife even during the community. Under these circumstances he gives part of his savings to his wife and the family income is divided in the proportion, let us say, of $6,000 to the man and $4,000 to the woman.
And under separation as to property?
Under separation as to property the exemption of $2,000 would apply on the man's $6,000, and the exemption of $2,000 would apply on the woman's $4,000.
My hon. friend will forgive me for interrupting him again. Under the income tax law a man cannot donate part of his income to his wife and claim exemption on that.

No, of course not but I am sure my hon. and learned friend in the course of his practice has come across many marriage contracts where, during the course of the marriage, the husband has the right to pay off the donation he makes to his wife at the time of the marriage. I am supposing a case where the husband does that and in which the wife acquires-as a gift from her husband or she may acquire it otherwise as a gift from a stranger-a property which brings a substantial annual income. Now, let us say that substantial annual income of $4,000 a year goes to the wife while the husband's income is $6,000 a year. In that case the total family income is $10,000 but it receives the benefit of two exemptions-one of $2,000 in respect of the man and another of $2,000 in respect of the woman.
It escapes the surtax also.

It escapes the surtax
also. The net result is that there are two citizens one of whom has been married under one regime and is paying substantially more taxation than another man with the same income who married under another regime. It seems to me that is an unfair way of applying income taxation. I remember discussing this matter with the late Sir Donald Mc-Master, who was a member of the British House, and who told me that in Great Britain -and there they have separation as to property-they regarded the income of the wife and the income of the husband as constituting for taxation purposes one income-subject to the exemptions that would accrue, but one income. Therefore it seems to me the min-

ister might take this into careful consideration, because I think most of us dislike paying taxes. Income taxes coming directly upon us have a certain pressure that some other taxes may not have; we have to pay, but one thing that will make us endure the income tax more readily than we otherwise would is the fact that it is levied in as fair a way as possible.

There is something in what my hon. friend says, and yet he does violence to a great many principles which should not be overlooked. I thought we had got to a point where we thoroughly recognized-and I am not speaking of Quebec, but of English Ontario-the rights of the married woman as the femme sole.
Oh, yes.

We have
extended to the woman, as far as I am concerned, every single right the man has. My hon. friend says you are to take it all from her, or take it all from the man, as the case may be. It would depend which has the larger income. I do not know as much about the law of Quebec as my hon. friend, but in Ontario we have marriage settlements and trust deeds which make absolutely inviolable the income of the wife. The husband cannot have anything to do with it at all. It is not his.
I do not propose that it should be regarded as his.

Her right is
absolute, and he has the absolute right of disposition of his income. I do not know how it would work out if you had a joint liability extending, when honest returns are made, to considerable figures, where under our act, you have that absolute right of disposition exercised by both the parties, and where the wife is supposed to be liable for the default of the husband, and the husband liable for default of the wife. That would follow from my hon. friend's statement, and is absolutely at variance with every canon of law in the country.
The law of the larger part of Great Britain is in principle similar to the law of Ontario, and that is the method.
I do not think the hon. member is right. Of course, it is the method, so far as the exemption is concerned. There is no necessity for two exemptions.
That is my main point.
There are not two exemptions; there is only one exemption.
Then that would mean that their incomes would be regarded as a joint income.

Not by any
manner of means. My hon. friend takes too much for granted altogether. They both have rights, and the best way for husband and wife to get along is to regard the rights of each other. I do not think the English law goes any further on the question of exemption. That is not a matter of the larger amount; it is more a question of the super tax. Will the minister tell me whether I am wrong in connection with the United States law? My recollection is that it is the same as ours.

In the United States there
are two incomes allowed, but only one exemption; but keep in mind that the one exemption in the United States is greater than the two exemptions in Canada.

I know that, but the two incomes are taxed. The woman's income in the vast majority of cases is an income from some trust estate; it is an investment which she has. As a general rule we do not find both husband and wife working. One thing I think we have all agreed on is that there is a limitation put upon the taxing power of this country. I do not know anyone who has looked into the subject fairly and honestly who has not come to that conclusion, and that limit to the taxing power is very, very apparent. To a very great extent, much more than we ought to be, we are compelled to pattern our legislation upon what our neighbours to the south do. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) nods his head-I am going to ask him, when he gives that assent, how is it practicable for us, in connection with the matter of income arising from investments almost entirely, to have a materially higher rate in connection with income than we have at present in this country. Of all things that can be moved income is one of the easiest. When you have your money coming in it is very easy to move; it does not take an awful lot to move it away and avoid the tax. This is going on all the time. If we were in a country or continent by ourselves, we would not be affected by that consideration. Australia can do things that we cannot do. I think every thoughtful man recognizes that one of the things that is going to worry the government a good deal is as to how they can hold what they

Why, Mr. Chairman, in connection with company taxation to-day, I venture the statement that 70 per cent, yes 75 per cent, of the companies paying under the income tax act to-day are paying far more than they would under the excess business profits tax. Under the excess profits tax provision there was no tax until 10 per cent had been earned. To-day it does not matter what dividend a company is paying, it has to pay a gross ten per cent income tax to the government. That is much heavier than could possibly be got under the old excess business profits tax if applied to-day. My hon. friend has his expert here, and if I am making any mistake, I want to be put right at once.
No mistake.

There is no
doubt about it. It is perfectly true. We are getting far more under the income tax to-day as we tax companies that gross ten per cent, than we could under the excess business profits tax. To-day, all the income taxes of companies are coming in under that heading. Before, they were represented in connection with the millions collected under the excess business profits tax, so that the real drop in the income of the regular individual taxpayer is infinitely greater than the drop shown between the figures of $81,000,000 and what we got last year, because when we got $81,000,000, we were at the same time getting $21,000,000 in excess business profits taxes from companies which now have to pay the 10 per cent income tax. The thing is dwindling.
The hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Caldwell) says that we should not have any sales tax and that we should get more from income tax. He wants to reduce exemptions and to make everybody pay. Again, there we can throw away money. There is no money whatever to the country in collecting small income taxes. A reasonable exemption is not the generous thing that hon. members might think it to be. The fact is that it does not pay to go to the cost of collecting the very small run of taxation; t'he state is out of pocket. There is a zone where that taxation can usefully be applied, and I do not see how anyone who believes in the integrity of the government can think that that zone can be very much increased at the present time. This is a form of taxation that this government, at least on the face of things, adopted, and' this was a good form of taxation, a form of taxation that hon. gentlemen to my left think a great

I would like to take this
opportunity of drawing to the attention of the minister the fact that the government are, I think, resorting to usury in charging delinquent income tax payers 10 per cent interest on arrears. I take it for granted' that most of these people who are in arrears cannot very well help themselves, and the government should make a change in the regulation which they are at present enforcing. The case which has been brought to my attention is that of a retailer who 'has been endeavouring for the last three years, or at least the last two years, to get his income tax paid up. He was assessed for income tax because his annual statement showed that he had goods on hand that really made him liable for income tax. But business was not very good for the next two years, and at the end of the two years he finds himself with a great proportion of those goods on the shelf, the value of them somewhat depreciated. In the meantime he has been paying interest on the money invested in his goods, and fire insurance on the goods, and he has not the cash to pay his income tax. He is being pressed for payment, of course, quite properly by the department occasionally, and he is being charged interest at the rate of 10 per cent. I do not think it is proper for the government to charge these people that rate of interest. Will the minister not see that that is changed; that these people should not be asked to pay 10 per cent interest.
Is a fine added to the 10 per cent when a man is delayed in paying his income tax?

No. The rule is that they pay 6 per cent on unpaid assessments, that is assessments that are paid at the time the return is put in. When the assessment is levied and proved by the department, the account finally closed, that is the time to settle. After that, they are charged 10 per cent. That is not an uncommon practice. That is a rule in nearly every municipality in connection with the imposition of municipal taxes. If you pay your taxes before a certain date, you pay so much. If you pass that date, you pay so much more. My hon. friend knows that. It is a common method in different municipalities in the assessment of their taxes. Our inspectors from western Canada tell us that unless we had that rate, people there would prefer paying off mortgages and other accounts to paying the government assessment of taxes. That is the reason for this imposition generally throughout Canada. No person is compelled to pay that 10 per cent if he pays up his taxes at once when they are levied.
Will the minister tell us about somebody in the West who could pay off a mortgage with his income tax?

No, but they use the money for that purpose. That is the experience of the department.
As regards the observations of the hon member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) as to the transfer of propertly from a husband to a wife, or a wife to a husband, to evade taxation, there is no such animal. Under the regulations:
A person who, after the 1st August, 1917, has reduced his income by the transfer or assignment of any real or personal, movable or immovable, property to such person, wife or husband as the case may be, or to any other member of the family, such person shall nevertheless be liable to the tax as if such transfer or assignment had not been made, unless the minister is satisfied that such transfer or assignment was not made for the purpose of evading the tax.

And they have lost that income through depreciation and carrying charges on the goods. They would be willing to pay the tax if they had the money, but they have not got it and

As income?

What is the law at present regarding the making out of forms? There are a great many who know that their incomes are not nearly sufficient to be taxable and who very often are put to a great deal of trouble trying to find out what ought to be done.

What constitutes such a
call?
A demand made by the department. But a man generally knows when he is liable and if he fails to make out his return he is liable to a penalty; in other words, he is running a risk.

There is a matter I want to bring to the attention of the minister. I do not know that this is a good day for getting changes made, but I want nevertheless to submit the facts as they came before me a short time ago. I admit that the circumstances were somewhat unusual. A gentleman wrote me stating that he had been
assessed for income tax and he asked me whether I thought the assessment was correct.
I wrote him that the decision of the department was absolutely in accordance with the law, but he felt that there was a hardship. He had a son who was over eighteen years of age but who was absolutely dependent upon him. The father was trying to give him the best education he could, keeping him at a university, and he felt, and I think not un naturally, that as he was actually dipping into the little bit of capital that he had accumulated in order to keep his boy at the university, he might be remitted the amount of the tax or given the allowance made in respect of dependent children under eighteen. Of course, the department could not do this; but I was impressed with the case as presented to me by this gentleman and I am passing it on to the minister in the hope that he may consider the advisability of adding some qualifying exemption so that in cases of real necessity where children are still dependent upon a parent, although they may be over eighteen years of age,-particularly in a case of this kind where a son is being educated at some institution of learning-some small remission may be granted.

Cases similar to this are
brought to our attention every week and we will take them all into consideration during the year.

But what do you do with them? What becomes of the consideration? Is it to find expression in the way in which the consideration will be shown which has been promised the hon. member for Brorne? Or is consideration effective when it is negotiated in the corridor and not across the floor?

I want to call the attention of the minister to what I think is a manifest case of injustice. Where a father has one or more children who because of physical or mental incapacity are totally unable to support themselves it would seem that there should foe a reasonable exemption from taxation even though these children may be over eighteen years of age, or even over, twenty-one. The law as it stands to-day, and as I understand it, does not provide for any allowance or deduction from the assessment of a parent on account of the support of such children, and I strongly urge that some such provision be made.

My hon. friend means that the parent of such children should be given the ordinary exemption allowed for children under eighteen years of age.

Yes, or some
special exemption.

These are the cases I had in mind when I told my hon. friend (Mr. Baxter) that representations were made to us every week. However, when we have the acts consolidated, as we hope to have them, all these matters will be considered.
But the act does not give any power in this case.

We propose making certain
amendments.
Representations have been made in the particular case I speak of but the objection is raised immediately that the act does not permit of anything being done.
Not now.

If a son is supporting a dependent father or mother, a parent who is entirely dependent upon him, does it make any difference, whether the son is married or single, as to whether or not he shall receive the exemption?

No; if the parent is entirely
dependent upon him the son is entitled to the exemption.

I want to ask the minister two questions. In the first place, what will be the loss of revenue as a result of this reduction? Further, I wrote the minister some time ago in connection with the question raised by the hon. member for Leeds, and I had in mind a pathetic case of a young woman whose father is not at all well to do. This woman is under thirty, or about thirty, and has been an inmate of hospitals for six or seven years and will doubtless be in the same condition more or less until she dies. I wrote to the minister regarding the matter and he replied to me by letter saying that he would consider it. I suppose that by reason of the amount of work he has to do he has forgotten all about it. Perhaps the matter was sent to the inspector of the department;
I do not know. However, the commissioner might probably be able to tell my hon. friend what conclusion has been arrived at in regard to such cases as this.

No, I recall the letter of my hon. friend. It is on file along with others for consideration. Of course, it is pretty hard to deal with the matter in a general statute. Power might be given to the minister or to the Treasury Board, but that would be a very dangerous proceeding, as I am sure my hon. friend will admit.

I agree; I would not give any power to the minister or to the board at all. But I see no reason why a very simple amendment could not be drafted which would cover the case of a permanent invalid child whom, irrespective of age, the parents have to look after at infinitely greater cost than in other circumstances.
We will keep it under consideration. I forgot to answer the other question asked by my hon. friend. I find that the estimated loss of revenue is $2,000000.
What! in connection with this exemption? Did my hon. friend have any idea there would be such a loss?
I am bound to say I did not.

DRAYTON:	On the one
hand we have a one minute talk on income taxation and the necessity of everybody paying; on the other hand we have dropping income tax receipts. Now we have a further exemption brought in which will cost the country $2,000,000 a year. Some hon. gentlemen, Mr. Chairman, when they are outside the House-and when they are in the House, unless there is some direct question of voting-are in favour of income taxation and making it just as certain as it can be made. I wonder what is the real opinion of those hon. gentlemen, in view of their general statements, when an amendment is proposed to grant exemptions which will run up to $2,000,000 a year? That is almost 4 per cent of the total income tax collected last year.
A little over 3 per cent.
It is nearer 4 per cent than 3 per cent. $55,000,000 was collected last year.
Yes; 3J per cent.
Shall the resolution carry?

I think, Mr. Chairman, that my hon. friend should tell us just what he thinks of this. He says the reduction is a surprise to him. Does he like to hand out $2,000,000-nearly 4 per cent of our income tax returns?

I am bound to say frankly,
Mr. Chairman, that I did not think the loss

of revenue would run up to $2,000,000. But, as intimated, the policy of the government is to reduce taxation, and we thought that a fair start in respect to income tax was to give some concession to those who have families, and we will have to stand by it.
Did I understand the minister to say that he would this session introduce an amendment to provide for the allowance in the case I discussed with him?

No, I said that I had the hon.
member's representations on file for consideration during the year.

Is there any
serious difficulty in bringing in a simple amendment to cover cases of this kind, leaving them to be dealt with by the minister or by the collector? I should think it could be dealt with in a few minutes, and would not interfere with any of the other provisions of the act. I think I could draft a simple amendment that would not cause any inconvenience.

I must point out to my hon.

The object of the proposed amendment is to overcome the effect of this 'technicality and to ensure that the Canadian treasury shall receive income tax upon profits made from Canadian business even although the formality of closing the deal takes place abroad.
As I understand, at present the only person you can tax is the local representative.
You can only tax him on his salary or commission.
He is taxable on his personal salary. But if there is nobody else here to tax, so far as the general business that he is carrying on is concerned, why is he not held now?

[.Sir Henry Drayton.]

And the article goes on to refer to some other items of a similar character.

It is alleged, for instance, that cheques totalling about $1,700,000, and representing the income and business profits taxes of three well-known concerns in Ontario, were received by the Department of Finance, of which Sir Henry Drayton was the then minister in March, 1921, but that they were not deposited until December 6 of that year. It is alleged that the synchcronizing of the election date-

I was remarking a few minutes ago that I drew the attention of the House to the specific case that had been submitted to me privately when I spoke on the budget on June 2, 1922, but that my doing so had not elicited any response from the Minister of Finance or from the government. At the end of the session, therefore, on June 29, 1922, I wrote the following letter to the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding):
You may recall a conversation which we had some weeks ago in regard to the answer made to certain questions which I had on the order paper. You stated,
I think on that occasion, that you would see Mr. Breadner and let me know the result of your interview with him. I did not hear anything from you and, subsequently, in my speech on the budget, gave detailed particulars in regard to one corporation which had apparently escaped the proper taxation. I thought that perhaps the specific figures which I gave in that case might lead to some reply on the part of the branch of the Finance department concerned; however, since the question has not been replied to, and the specific case ignored, I am taking this opportunity of calling your attention again to what seems to me a matter of very considerable importance.
I proceeded at some length in the letter to outline the situation and in conclusion I said:
I hope that you will look into this matter at your earliest convenience, as I feel sure, from what information has reached me, that some investigation and some real clean-up is highly desirable.
I am sending a copy of this letter to the Premier, Mr. Mackenzie King.

I sent a copy of the letter to the Prime Minister.	.
I did not hear from the Minister of Finance in reply until January 22, 1923, on which date he wrote me as follows:
Referring to your letter of the 29th June, 1922, concerning a certain assessment under The Business Profits War Tax Act, in view of your expressed dissatisfaction with the decision reached by Mr. R. W. Breadner, Commissioner of Taxation, I deemed it expedient to have an independent inquiry made. For the purpose, I had the matter placed in the hands of Mr. George Edwards, of the firm of Edwards, Morgan and Company, chartered accountants, whose services had already been engaged for other departmental work. I now send you a copy of Mr. Edwards' report. You will notice that it is dated November 24, 1922. I should explain, however, that it only came before me since my return from Europe a few days ago.
Enclosed with the letter was the report from Mr. Edwards which I have in my hand. In this report Mr. Edwards deals in detail with the specific case, without mentioning the name of the company concerned. I shall read one or two extracts from the report.
Comparing the figures, I note that the share capital is correctly stated at $250,000 but the reserves amount to $5,731,350.20 or exactly $5,000,000 more than reported in Hansard. The gross profits are correctly stated at $1,571,626.17, but after deducting income tax, inventory adjustments and depletion allowances, the balance or net profit remaining is $1,086,573.23, an amount which is less by $337,191.08 than reported in Hansard. The actual assessment is correctly stated at $214,312.36. From the foregoing it will be evident that the suggestion of an under assessment is based upon information which is incomplete and in part incorrect. The capital employed is $5,000,000 greater, and the profits in this particular year were some $337,000 less. Upon the statements of fact presented by the departmental files, the amount assessed has been correctly computed.
He goes on to say that he personally visited the office of the company, and further on the report states:
It will be noted, therefore, that no occasion has arisen for determining the constantly accumulating value of the capital assets of the company, until required to do so by the provisions of The Business Profits War Tax Act. No books, other than the statutory books, and a cash book had been found necessary and therefore apparently no others had been kept.
The report, which continues at considerable length, is an endorsation of the assessment made by the department. When I received it I submitted it to my original informant who was a gentleman in the city well acquainted with the administration of the Business Profits War Tax Act; and after discussing it with me he gave me a memorandum which I should like to present to the House.

Will the hon.
gentleman have any objection to saying who wrote the memorandum?

What does the
Chairman rule as to the reading of an anonymous memorandum?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member
may read from a memorandum without giving the author's name. The rule applies only to a minister who reads from a public document; it requires him to read the whole document and to disclose the author. The rule does not apply to private members.

If there is any objection to
my reading the memorandum, Mr. Chairman, I will simply give the substance of it.
I have no objection, only I should like to know who is the author.

I do not think its authorship
makes very much difference. It is the argument contained in it which I should like to submit to the House.
Read it.

This is the memorandum:
The report of Mr. Edwards, chartered accountant, on this matter, shows that the difference between my information and his is that he puts in the reserves $5,000,000 more than I do. There is no mention in the report what this reserve of $5,000,000 consists of. I would judge, however, from the latter part of his report that the department and Mr. Edwards have determined or have fixed the value of the mine of the company at $5,000,000 and class it as a reserve.
It is quite evident that this is merely an accountant's method of avoiding the business profits war tax. I would be very glad, if you thought it advisable, to discuss the matter with Mr. Edwards, as he may be able to convince me that there is some provision in the business profits war tax that allows a company to add $5,000,000 for the value of its mine, but I must confess that a somewhat careful examination of the act and the amendments does not show me any provision that can be so construed.
The business profits war tax, section 3, provides, there shall be levied and paid to His Majesty a tax of 25 per cent of the amount by which the profit earned in any business exceeded in the case of a business owned by an incorporated company the rate of 7 per cent per annum upon the capital employed in such business. The 25 per cent was amended subsequently. Then the word "profits" is defined in section 6 as the net profits, with a provision that the minister when determining the profits derived shall make an allowance for the exhaustion of the mines. "Capital" is defined by section 7 as being, "The amount paid up on its capital stock."
Then the definition of "capital stock" is given, and there is some further explanation and quotations from the act.
The memorandum proceeds:
Subsection 4 then provides that reserves may be included in the capital. The words are "the actual unimpaired reserve, rest or accumulated profits of an incorporated company shall be included as part of its capital." These words have no application to the value of what Mr. Edwards calls "the capital assets".
Reserves are savings set aside for various purposes and not distributed in dividends to the shareholders. Capital assets are the assets for which the capital stock stands.
That is all that is material to the point I am making. Then I have before me the two statements, the original submitted to me on which I based some of my questions, and the amended statement which was endorsed by Mr. Edwards. The main distinction between the two statements is that in the one case there is $5,000,000 allowed for the value of the mine, and in the other case there is not. The point which hon. members should grasp is that by the allowance of $5,000,000 for the value of the mine the very large exemption of 7 per cent could be claimed, which would allow this particular concern to pay about $200,000 instead of about a million dollars which they were liable for under the other construction. I do not need to go into the statements in detail. I have them here if any hon. member wants to look over them.
What is the point?

The point will be apparent
very soon, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. gentleman cannot see it now.

We have been waiting
for it a long time.

On Feb. 8 of last year I wrote to Mr, Fielding. The substance of my letter was that I was not satisfied with the report of Mr. Edwards and desired to discuss the matter with him in the expectation that possibly he would be able to clear up some of the mysteries that seemed to surround this case. I also asked for permission to look into the particular file. Mr. Fielding wrote me on February' 9 as follows:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of 8th instant in relation to the income tax matter concerning which we have had some correspondence.
Mr. Edwards has been in Ottawa for several days, but has returned to Toronto. I will communicate with him and ask him when he is again in Ottawa to call and see you.
In reply, I wrote to Mr. Fielding calling bis attention to the fact that he had not said anything about my getting access to the file in question. Writing to me on February 20 he told me that Mr. Edwards was in town that day and would call and see me, but that the files were not accessible to the public and that therefore I would not be at liberty to examine this particular file.
Mr. Edwards called to see me shortly afterwards. I had a long discussion with him and we went into the case in detail. I discovered that he justified the assessment on different grounds from those upon which he had justi-



Ways and Means-Income Tax
fied it in his memorandum. This was his summing up of the condition of this particular concern:
$250,000-original investment 45 years ago.
$431,000-stock of merchandise on hand 1918.
$2,000,000-buildings, equipment, etc.
$3,300,000-value of mine.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I cannot see any justification in the act for the allowance of $3,300,000 for the value of the mine. You will observe that in the former communication $5,000,000 was allowed as the value. On discussing the matter with Mr. Edwards he divided the property into the plant and the mine, and he said the value of the plant, which to some extent might be counted as a reserve, was in his opinion about $2,000,000, and the value of the mine he put in as $3,300,000. I inquired as to the justification for this, and his argument was, roughly, that what seemed to be a bona fide offer for the property had been made some years ago of about $6,000,000, and that if any attempt were made to place the valuation too low the company could easily go through a form of sale to establish a higher valuation for the property, and he could not see how the higher assessment could have been enforced under the act. Thus he confirmed his original opinion as to the assessment, although he based it on somewhat different grounds. I may say that the discussion I had with him was very satisfactory from the point of view of getting information, and I left the case in that position towards the end of last session.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take up the time of the committee much longer with regard to this matter, but I would call attention again to the charges made in the three Globe articles, which I think are sufficiently serious to demand on the part of this House a thorough investigation by the government into the administration of this department. I have no interest in this matter from a party point of view. Possibly the Globe has; if the ex-Minister of Finance thinks that the Globe is trying to make party capital he is entitled to that opinion and there may be something in it; I do not care a rap for that. But my own investigation has suggested to me that in connection with the administration of these acts- whether or not too much latitude has been allowed I cannot say-there is very much that we should know, very much that we do not know, and I am going to ask that a thorough investigation be made into this whole matter in order to prove or disprove the charges made in the three articles in the Globe and to throw light upon the adminis-

tration of these acts. I am moreover not satisfied with the explanations which I finally got from Mr. Edwards through the department in the particular case cited. It was one case out of possibly a great many cases. I say I am not satisfied; but at the same time I do not wish to make any- charges as to the violation of the law, though it would seem to me that t'he law has been violated. I say I would like a thorough investigation to determine whether there has been any violation of the law and to expose the violation if there has been any; if not, then to establish that justice has been done to all parties. If the allegations made in the Globe are correct, or anywhere near correct, the country has lost a tremendous amount of revenue running to about $800,000 in the particular case I have mentioned. I ask the Minister of Finance and I ask the government to institute a thorough investigation into the administration of this department.

The question under consideration is the income tax, and under that head my hon. friend has brought up the question of the administration of the business profits tax and the income tax. My hon. friend was not a member of this House when that legislation was put through. I am not sure whether had he been a member of the House he would have taken the attitude that most hon. members took at that time, namely that secrecy was the essence of the act. It was pointed out by many hon. members from all parts of Canada when the act was first introduced that one of the results of its operation would be that every man's business would be known to his competitors and that unfair dealing would follow. A pledge was given by the then Finance Minister-and it was put in the act- that there w-as to be secrecy as to the returns filed with the department regarding the business and the revenues of people throughout the country. Until recently, so far as I know, that, generally speaking, has been fairly well observed, but it is apparent that in some ways certain information coming into the department is leaking out, with a consequent disturbing effect in the country. Though I have been Acting Minister of Finance for some months I have never taken advantage-and under the act the minister is a member of the taxation commission-of that information in order to dig into any man's business.
In the first place my hon. friend brings up the question as it affects a mining corporation, I think it was, and he referred to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in that connection. Mr. Fielding, acting upon information given to him by the hon. member

for Brant, employed a chartered accountant, one who is recognized in all parts of Canada as at the head of his profession. That chartered accountant went very carefully into the matter, visited the mine and submitted a report to the minister. Associated with Mr. Edwards was Mr. Hutchison, of Riddell, Steed and Hutchison of Montreal, so that we have the statement of two reputable chartered accountants who, on instructions of the Minister of Finance, went carefully into the reports as filed with the department. My hon. friend has read part of the report to the minister in that connection; I think I might as well put it all on Hansard so that hon. members of the House and the people of the country will have it before them. It is dated November 24, 1922 and is as follows:
The Honourable,
The Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge your instructions to investigate the circumstances respecting an asessment made under the provisions of the Business Profits War Tax Act 1910, to which reference was made by Mr. Good, M.P., in the House of Commons, and reported in Hansard No. 55, 2nd June 1922, as fallows:
"A certain company in a certain year had a capital stock, according to this statement, as follows: $250,000; reserves, $731,350.20, making a total capital employed of $981,350.20. The gross profit of that company, according to the statement submitted, was, I am told, $1,571,626.17. Deducting from that the income tax-I will not read the figures; I have them here-the decrease in the inventory and the depletion, I find there is left a net profit of $1,423,764.31. According to the act, I am informed that the assessment levied on that company in that particular year should have been $1,111,983.99, made up as follows: 7 per cent of the capital employed, exempt from taxation; 8 per cent, one-quarter taken by the government; 5 per cent, of capital employed, one-half taken by the government and of the balance of profits, which was considerably over $1,000,000, six-sevenths should have come into the federal treasury. The total assessment which, according to this statement, ought to have been levied on that particular company, was considerably over $1,000,000. What was the actual assessment by the department?- $214,312.36. In connection with this one company for one year, if these figures are correct, and if there is no good justification for the action which the department has taken, there is an apparent loss to the country of $897,671.63."
That was the statement placed on Hansard by the hon. member for Brant, referred to by Mr. Edwards in his report to the minister on the date which I have given. Then follows his report:
I have been supplied by the Department of Taxation, at your request, with the files relating to a mining company, an examination of which identifies this company with the one referred to by the member. Comparing the figures, I note that the share capital is correctly stated at $250,000, but the reserves amount to $5,731,350.20 or exactly $5,000,000 more than reported in Hansard.
The gross profits are correctly stated at $1,571,626.17 but, after deducting income tax, inventory adjust-

ments and depletion allowances, the balance or net profit remaining is $1,086,573.23, an amount which is less by $337,191.08 than reported in Hansard. The actual assessment is correctly stated at $214,312.36. From the foregoing it will be evident that the suggestion of an under assessment is based upon information which is incomplete and in part incorrect. The capital employed is $5,000,000 greater, and the profits in this particular year were some $337,000 less. Upon the statements of fact presented by the departmental files, the amount assessed has been correctly computed.
I have personally visited the office of this company, which is located at the mines, where also all the operations are carried on. I have been afforded every facility for forming an independent opinion upon the questions involved. The auditors of the company, a firm of the highest repute, have given to me their certified statements and reports upon the company's position.
The company was incorporated in 1877, and has therefore operated fox 45 years. During that time there has been no change of share ownership, the present shareholders being either the original proprietors or their estates, and their respective interests are likewise unchanged. During this entire period the policy has been maintained of distributing periodically to the shareholders, the cash balances remaining on hand after making all necessary expenditures, including capital charges for development, plant and other facilities. It will be noted, therefore, that no occasion has arisen for determining the constantly accumulating value of the capital assets of the company, until required to do so by the provisions of the Business Profits War Tax Act. No books, other than the statutory books, and a cash book have been found necessary and therefore apparently no others had been kept.
It is evident from the statements I have obtained from the officers of the company, the auditors, and the officers of the Department of Taxation, that a sincere effort was made to arrive at a fair and just decision as to the value which should be placed upon the company's physical assets for taxation purposes in accordance with the conditions prescribed by the act. The prescription applicable to this case is contained in subsection 4 of section 7, which reads as follows:
(7) (4) For the purposes of this act, the actual unimpaired reserve, rest or accumulated profits held at the commencement of an accounting period by an incorporated company, shall be included as part of its capital as long as it is held and used by the company as capital, and dividends paid during an accounting period shall be considered as a reduction of unimpaired reserve, rest or accumulated profits.
Then Mr. Edwards continues:
I have taken the statements separately of the persons who took part in the inquiry and these statements are in substantial agreement. A competent departmental officer was deputed to visit the company's office and make a report. Similar reports were procured respecting other mining companies producing like commodities, and comparative data was thus obtained. The representatives of these companies were then invited to Ottawa in turn to confer with a view to reaching a reasonable basis for determining capital. I have asked for and have been given access to the files of the department dealing with the cases of a number of these companies. For the most part they had changed hands one or more times within a comparatively few years, and it was possible therefore to test fairly well the true commercial value of the classes of physical assets which they had in common. There was no other possible method of determining the extent of the company's reserves.
I am quite convinced from the evidence I have examined, and from an inspection of the physical assets of
