Yours very truly,
George Edwards,
Chartered Accountant.
That report was endorsed by Mr. Hutchinson, of Riddell, Stead & Hutchison. Now, what more could' the Finance Minister have done? My hon. friend (Mr. Good) finds some fault with what was done. Well, hon. gentlemen all know the Minister of Finance as well as I do and unless it was absolutely necessary he would not have allowed-

May I correct the minister?
When I made the request to examine the files I did not know they were considered confidential. I had no objection, and did not register any objection, whatever, to being denied access to the files when the minister told me they were regarded as confidential; nor did I express any dissatisfaction with the minister for undertaking the investigation- instructing Mr. Edwards to make the investigation. I think he did the only thing he could do under the circumstances, and I have no objection to that at all.

I am very glad to have that
statement from my hon. friend. I was going on to say that I gathered1-it may be incorrectly-that he was rather finding fault because he had not been given access to the files.
No.

I was going on to say that
to grant access to the files would not only have been a breach of faith, it would have been a breach of trust. It is true my hon. friend makes no charges. He does, however, make what might be termed insinuations that the department were not fairly administering the act. We have before us the report of a chartered accountant engaged, by the Minister of Finance to go carefully into 
the matter, and that chartered accountant certified to the minister that the assessment was properly made in that case.
Now we come to the items that were published in the Toronto Globe. No names were mentioned in the Globe but I think I may as well put these statements on record. This is an extract from the Globe of 25th February, 1924:
1.	A thorough probe it is stated would reveal that one prominent Toronto concern was assessed in July, 1921, to be taxed by over $60,000, but that the notice of assessment was held until late in December of that year, no interest being collected or charged for the lapsed time.
2.	Another Toronto company it is alleged had its assessment reduced by $18,000 principally through extra salary allowances. This assessment was made in April, 1921, and the company paid on the instalment plan $2,000 monthly. It's notice of assessment was sent out in August, 1922, no interest being charged or collected as the notice was withheld until the instalments were completed.
Now as to case No. 1 there is sufficient in the article to determine just about who they were. I do not know who they were but I have the statement from the record that the capital was $907,190.85. The profits as reported in returns and as set forth in the auditor's statement signed by Edwards, Morgan and Company, chartered accountants of Toronto, were $154,375.93. The tax collected on the above figures would amount to $27,292.46, but the tax levied by the department was not $27,292.46 but $61,926.68. So that the House will observe that they were assessed for more than their chartered accountants claimed they should be; and there is no suggestion in this House that the statements of the chartered accountants or of the company are not reliable. The comparison is merely for the purpose of showing that the Dominion exchequer has benefited to the extent of approximately $57,000 in two years from what the taxpayer himself considered his liability.
In regard to No. 2, in this concern the capital was, $373,289.07. and the profits, after deducting depreciation and reasonable salaries were $79,326.13. The assessment based on those figures would be $20,301.34, but the department levied a tax of $36,051.35. So that, in addition, on account of salary adjustments, further assessments to the extent of $976.80 were levied against the individuals under the income war tax. I mention this to show that the reports, in so far as the companies are concerned, were not justified. Every person knows that the tax collector in a community, whether it be a municipal tax collector or a school municipal collector, or any tax collector, is not the most popular man in the country; and the Commissioner of Taxation

for Canada possibly has not earned popularity among many people who are compelled to pay taxes. But I desire to say that this government and the Commissioner of Taxation have nothing to hide, and if any gentleman has the courage to make any charges and to submit them to the Public Accounts committee, they will be thoroughly examined and gone into, and he will have permission to bring his witnesses before that committee.

The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) has perhaps fallen into a very natural error. He does not know, for example, the Globe as well as some of us know it; and he is in the unfortunate position of having confused Philip Drunk with Philip Sober. He is exactly acting on the position taken by some at least of the present occupants of the treasury benches when they were not Philip Sober. He is remembering the wild and silly charges that were made in regard to the Riordon case. He is remembering that in that campaign it was said that as soon as the government came into power there was to be an investigation, which I have been courting ever since. But he has forgotten that sometimes the wildest insanity becomes sanity; and after all there is a morning after the night before. And to-day the government are charged with carrying out the laws of this country. They are not concerned to-day with making improper and false statements as to political opponents and what they have done. They are concerned with carrying out the law. At that time they and the papers supporting them were concerned in saying that the very sections that the hon. the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has properly referred to to-night were framed for the purpose of protecting Drayton. But as I say that is gone; they are in a position of responsibility now. I have always courted an investigation and I do so now. My position now is just as it was then. There ought to be regard for law and regard for the statute. There ought to be regard for the confidence of the ratepayer, and it is for the government to say whether it is to be violated or not.
So far as this particular case is concerned, my hon. friend is again in an unfortunate position. He has relied upon the Globe, and the first case he cites shows that the Globe has been interested in running down some Toronto ratepayer. I do not know how this information was obtained; but I do know that the ratepayers of this country are going to be interested in finding out why it is that some newspaper or some people can gain access to confidential documents. That is a breach of the law, and a breach of
the situation as described by the Acting Minister of Finance. Somebody has been giving information but from the date of the assessment, and although I do not know what it was, I should imagine it was still the same old game of trying in some way or other to show something wrong was done in 1921. I would assume it is for that purpose, and, as it appears in the Globe, my assumption is altogether more likely to be correct. But there is a place where there might be an investigation. What chance has the honest man in business to get along properly if perchance his competitor here or his competitor there is allowed to obtain knowledge of everything he is doing and his resources and salaries? If it be open for the Globe in some way or other to get these particulars, why is it not open to anybody else? Well, my hon. friend is wrong, because he again trusted the Gldbe. We see, according to a report given to the acting minister, that as a result of the delays which took place for the purpose of ascertaining the truth, making proper valuations, and writing up values where values were written down, the tax in the first instance referred to is raised from $27,000 to $61,000. Was the delay not worth it? Was the department not doing the right thing in writing up the values and obtaining a true knowledge of the situation?
The second case he refers to is not very much more fortunate. How did the delay work out there? It has been alleged that the assessment was not made soon enough. Fancy anyone talking about interest on an improper amount of $20,000 as a matter of loss, when we find that, as a result of the delay and of getting the actual value, instead of the country getting $20,000 it got $36,000. There is the whole situation. I have a good deal of sympathy for my hon. friend from Brant. He has been misled. He has become mixed up with Philip Drunk and Philip Sober. He has become mixed up with the Globe and the family Bible, but I will say again, as I have said more than once,-and this has been corroborated both by the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) from his place in this House and by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb)-that there is nothing to bide in this matter, so far at any rate as one Drayton is concerned, and that I look for an investigation, if anyone is rash enough to bring it on. I have absolutely nothing to hide. My position is just as it was before. Then I was bound by the ordinary decencies of public life to keep quiet. I could not give the details. I had no right to do so. The details now are with hon. gentlemen on

the other side. Any breach of decency today will not be my 'breach, and if they want to make that breach, I can assure them that so far as I personally am concerned, I will welcome an investigation.

In regard to the case which I mentioned, which has been referred to by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), I should like to make my position absolutely clear, because I am afraid that it has been misunderstood. I have no desire to question Mr. Edwards' ability as an accountant, but I want to state very frankly that I can see no justification for the conclusion to which he came. It may be my fault, but I submit to the committee that, under the act, there seemed to be no justification for the allowance of $5,000,000 that was made. The further explanation made to me personally by Mr. Edwards divided that amount into an allowance for the plant, for which allowance there might be some justification, and a very large allowance for the value of the mine, for which allowance I can see under the act no justification whatever. The section quoted by Mr. Edwards, subsection 4 of section 7 reads:
For the purposes of this act the actual unimpaired reserve, rest or accumulated profits of an incorporated company shall be included as part of its capital.
If the value of the plant is to be taken as the accumulated profits-and I suppose it is in this case; what were not paid out to the shareholders as dividends were put into the plant-the reserve, so to speak, then that is all that can be allowed for and what can be said about the allowance that both the department and Mr. Edwards justify of over three million dollars, at least, for the mine.
That is the capital.

The capital is defined under
the act as being not more than the par value of the capital stock, $250,000, which is negligible in this case. I ask the government to make an investigation. I am sorry if, in any way, I should be party to such an investigation as will throw into discredit any particular person or persons. I regret that, in a matter of this sort, certain persons seem to be, necessarily, reflected upon. I cannot help that; there is no way of avoiding it; but I think there is a sufficient amount of information now evident to require an investigation by the government. If it is desirable to have a private investigation, let the government assume responsibility for whatever kind of investigation they see fit to institute. But I contend that the information which we have already secured and the charges, if such
[Sir Henry Drayton.)
they may be taken to be, contained in the Globe articles are sufficient to require an investigation. In fact, I would think it is highly desirable to clear up the charges and not to allow them to stand there as suggestions and insinuations, if you like, against the probity of certain persons in this House and elsewhere. Should they not be cleared up? I do not wish to be considered as desiring to reflect discredit upon any individual; but I feel that in this particular case a certain favouritism has been exercised towards a particular concern, a concern which made profits amounting to a million and a half dollars in one year, whereas, the country at that time secured only about $200,000 of taxes out of $1,500,000 profits from a company that started with $250,000 of a capital and which had, at most, according to Mr. Edwards' statement to me, about $2,000,000 worth of a plant. I submit to members of the committee that something seems to be wrong with that. Let it be investigated. I am only calling for an investigation, and I think it is up to the government to provide for an investigation of whatever kind they think most suitable

Do I understand that the

What the hon.
member says about capital does not come under that particular act. It is not the amount of the face capital at all. Very often the face capital is ever so much more than ought to be deducted. On the other hand, when the face capital is nominal, manifestly you have to apply the same rule. What you have to arrive at is the value of the vehicle that is producing the results. That is putting the matter in a rough way, but that is really what it is. Never mind about the paper capital or the paper reserve. What is the real value of the thing used? Mr. Edwards says that the real value is this $5,000,000, and he also says, as regards the real value, that it was offered for $6,000,000. If my hon. friend will look at this particular act, he will see that the ordinary rule does not apply.

I would ask the hon.
member (Sir Henry Drayton), as he was once responsible for the administration of this act, to consider whether the act cited by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) contemplates this fixing of the value of the assets at their real value. It would almost appear by the citation from the act made by the hon. member for Brant, that, the capital must be the capital of the company and not the real value of the property.

I can assure my hon. friend that it would have been a very easy act to administer if that had been the case, and the returns in the great majority of cases would have been very small. We have watered capital, and if that reading were to be given to the act, many companies, that had to pay heavy rates would have got off with nominal taxation. We had to do that in order to get revenue, and that meant going into the whole thing and finding out what real values were.

Is the real difficulty in this case not a difficulty of legal interpretation of the act? It seems to me that that is where the difficulty comes in. If, under the act, the taxing power had the right to assess what was the real value of the property producing the income, then it occurs every day, especially in companies that are owned in a family, that the nominal capital may bear no relation to the real value of the property. If under the act the assessment could be computed upon the real value of the property then it appears to me the difficulty might disappear altogether. I have never examined
the matter as a practising lawyer with any [DOT]great care and I should be gladi to hear from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), if he has looked into it, as to whether it is proper under the act to compute the rate of taxable profits not upon the nominal capital but upon the real value of the institution.
That is what we did at any rate; we took the real value.

The section we are discussing is as follows:
For certain modifications of the present law pertaining to the income tax lien and to render certain that the lien shall not take priority over securities validly taken to the time at which the lien attaches.
I want to enter as strong a protest as I can against the department taking a lien against the property of a taxpayer, which lien, could, by any possibility take priority over existing securities. This section states that there are to be certain modifications. I do not want to continue the discussion unduly if the proposed modifications will meet the situation, and I would therefore ask the Acting Minister of Finance to indicate just what those modifications are to be.

Perhaps the hon. member will recall that when this amendment to the act came up last year under section 25 I raised the most strenuous objections to its being put into effect at that time; and finally, after many solicitations, I induced the Minister of Finance to put over the operation of that particular section until the accounting period of 1924, that is to say, around May 1, 1925, the income tax statements being submitted, as my hon. friend is aware, on April 30, 1925. That section last year constituted a lien on all property movable or immovable of the tax payer over all assessments made or to be made; that is to say, the income tax created a lien ranking prior to a mortgage	or even a sale, irrespective	of
whether the income tax was assessed before or after the security was created. And that in my opinion was a very unfair attitude for the department to take. The amendment now submitted by the Acting Minister of Finance changes that completely, providing that the income tax lien will take effect and be a lien only in relation to that part of the tax which is assessed before the execution of any particular security such as a mortgage, a conveyance or a collateral security.

Is my hon. friend speaking for the Acting Minister of Finance? I dto not know, but apparently he is familiar with the nature of the probable modifications.

He is trying to enlighten the House.
I understand that quite well.
Does the hon. gentleman think that the Anting Minister of Finance alone can interpret the section?

Certainly not; but I do think that the committee is entitled to an explanation from the Acting Minister himself. It makes no difference to me however where that explanation comes from so long as I am assured that the statement which the hon. member is making is an indication of what the minister intends to do.

For the information of my hon. friend I want to say that, naturally, I am not speaking for the government. I am speaking for a reason which I shall state; and perhaps the hon. member will not consider me impertinent for undertaking to offer a word of explanation in regard to the section.
I did not mean to be rude to my hon. friend; all I wanted to know was whether what he has suggested are the proposed modifications which are ultimately to be submitted by the acting minister.

I am speaking for this
reason. Last year I raised strong objections to the enactment of a section similar to this, and I have been taking up this particular question with the department with a view to having a clause passed which would seem to me to be fair both to the department and to the public at large. This matter has been brought to my attention by very many persons in Toronto, in Montreal and in various other parts of the Dominion; and this owing largely, in fact entirely, to my having offered the objection I did last year, when my remarks were published in Hansard. For that reason alone, and not because I consider myself an authority on the subject, I have undertaken to refer to the subject. In my opinion the suggested amendment is a fair one inasmuch as it only allows the unpaid income tax assessed prior to the execution of a security to rank as a lien on taxable property. In other words, a mortgage being registered on a certain day and income tax being clear up to that date, then the creditor has no necessity to examine the income tax statement of the debtor after the registration of the mortgage; and provision is made by the department so that the usual waivers or certificates, or whatever you choose to call them, will be issued on demand, showing that there is nothing owing by the debtor mortgaging or selling a security.

There seems to be an evident desire on both sides of the House to change the subject, but I want to add a word in conclusion to what I said before regarding the matter I have already brought up. So far as the particular case which I personally investigated is concerned, I am not attaching a tremendous amount of importance to it, but I want to tell the committee frankly that I see no justification for what was done. The contention may be made that one could not keep to the act, that one had to violate it, in that it was not fair. If the officials take that view then perhaps the action taken can be justified on that basis. Nevertheless, I submit that the act was violated in this particular case. As I have remarked, however, I do not attach supreme importance to this case because there may be some extenuating circumstances that would seem to justify it, although personally I cannot see it. But I do think that in view of the subsequent charges, of a very serious and very varied character, made by the Globe, some action should be taken. Am I to understand that the government has investigated all the allegations made in the Globe articles, and in consequence denounces them as untrue? If that is the case, and the House is to be given to understand that these things have all been investigated, and if the government declares them to be baseless, I personally shall be well satisfied and pleased to know that things are properly conducted. I ask the Acting Minister of Finance to make a statement now that these matters have all been inquired into and that the government is satisfied that everything is O.K.

I repeat that from the items as they appeared in the Toronto Globe we were able fairly to trace tue accounts, and I have read to the committee a statement of account to show that the Globe was very much misinformed. I should like to return to the resolution. I do not want to be discourteous to my hon. friend but I have already told him that the Public Accounts are open to any member of the House and that the government will welcome any investigation into any department of the public service which hon. members may wish to make before the Public Accounts committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The staff is being reduced at the rate on an average of about 20 a week, and one must bear in mind that of the main staff of the department a proportion, I think 95 per cent, are returned men, and a proportion again are disabled men. The purpose of the department is to exercise all possible care and diligence in reducing the staff. The employees receive notification in advance; and in the meantime, before the date arrives when they shall be released, we undertake to do everything possible in order to secure employment for them. Many of our employees are disabled to an extent that we feel sometimes that it is the duty of the department, of the government and of the country to keep them a little while longer, and I venture to say that it will not be possible at any time in the future to reduce the staff at a faster rate than 20 a week, or about 75 a month, or 900 to 1,000 a year. If we continued to reduce the staff at that rate it would mean that in three or four years they would all have been let out. Although I do not think, perhaps, the department should remain as it is to-day, I believe that it will require two or three years before the number of employees will be reduced to such a point that it will not be worth mentioning. At one time the staff was composed of pretty nearly 9,000, and if we include the work of the pension commissioners it was at that time 10,000. In 1921 I think all the staff of the Board of Pension Commissioners was taken over by this department, and from that time the department has been reducing constantly at the rate on an average of 1,000 a year, or even more, and I submit we are doing fairly well. We may not reduce the staff as rapidly as my hon. friend would wish, perhaps, but were he in my place, knowing his heart, and his good nature, I can assure him that he would not reduce the staff any faster. Representations have been made to me by men who are deserving, men who have done brilliant service, and men who have suffered disability, the heads of families, and so on, and we exercise all possible care when it comes to dispensing with their services. Nothing would please me more than to reduce the expenditure further.

The people of Canada expect that the government will not shelter themselves behind any technicality or code of rules in regard to their treatment of these men. A g:eat deal of complaint has been made since last session about the administration of this particular branch of the department. When we considered this item previously there were some co-ordinations and some consolidations made which might account for the difference. I refer to the Smith case, Mr. Smith being a soldier resident in Davisville near Toronto. The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) is not here to-night. He intended to take it up. Then there is the Strickland case, Strickland being a destitute soldier, the Taylor case, a soldier on Portland Street and some others. These gentlemen come under this particular vote. The doctors examined them and I have a lot of correspondence with the department in regard to them. The civilian doctors, of repute, who had considerable experience, and who examined these men, do not agree with the DjS.C.R. board of medical men. The

best the country can do for these soldiers is none too good for them. They are not going to live forever, and they are dying off by hundreds. Many of them have been struck off the pension rolls on technicalities and the number averages about 4,307. At page 671 of last year's Hansard the minister gave for the years 1919-22 and 1922-23 the details of the number of cases and he has repeated these details to-night, and 'added those for 1924. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction in the city I come from, and the ladies' organizations with the city government and the board of trade and other civic organizations had to get together during the dark days of January, February, March and April to obtain assistance for soldiers in need and distress by way of a tag day. Many of them were without work, they and their families were without food and clothing and some could not obtain medical treatment. The ex-service men and the different associations, the board of trade, and the city treasurer did what they could. The members of the various patriotic funds and other organizations had to be recalled, and they organized a campaign and parties went around from door to door in Toronto and collected $48,000. which the people of Canada should have contributed. I would like the minister to tell us about the care and treatment of these cases at present in the hospitals and the medical examination of the men. In many cases the applications for pensions or aid for these men were thrown out or curtailed. I mentioned three cases to-night. Then there is the case of Pte. Boxall. Lieutenant Colonel Campbell, an overseas soldier, came to me with a pile of papers to-day and the file re this Boxall case. Boxall was a returned soldier. His oase has been ruled out by the department on some technicality. This man contracted his disease overseas and the department's doctors ruled him out although five or six civilian doctors backed up his statement that he should receive a pension.
There is too much red tape in the administration of this department in their treatment of the soldiers in the city from which I come. The Christie Street hosptial is the largest hospital in Canada for the treatment of soldiers, and they are doing splendid work. The minister's heart is in the work, and he has my sympathy and support. The findings of the Ralston commission should be brought up to date, there should be no delay in bringing in their final report and the relief set out therein should be brought into effect at once. In many instances the doctors of the department rule cut cases, while civilian doctors of
good professional ability certify to the contrary as to the facts in individual cases, and with all respect to the department, I think something should be done to take care of these men denied a pension by red tape. There should be a more liberal interpretation of the act. The soldiers are dying by tens, twenties and thirties in Toronto and Ontario every month. They are not going to live for ever or to be a drag on the government for all time. Last year the estimates of this department were $14,000,000. This year the amount has been reduced to $9,000,000, a reduction of $5,000,000. Next year, if we have a proportionate reduction, the estimates will amount to about $5,000,000. This department shows a reduction of about 37}- per cent. Is this the only department that is going to be cut down in that way and singled out for economy? One-half of the estimates goes for administration. The minister's figures may be all right as to the number treated. The Ralston commission went over the whole of Canada and it made two reports. One report was brought down the other day, and it is about time that we had the final report and put it all into effect. Let us have the facts and find out how many men have been struck off the books, turned on a cold, uncharitable world for a living, without anything, and allowed to shift for themselves. You cannot expect these men to be 100 per cent efficient after spending two, three or four years overseas. Some people will not give them a position and the country owes them a proper pension.
As regards the amputation cases, getting $75 a month, I know of a young soldier, a hardworking man, an amputation case. He has two arms off, and he cannot get any work. After weeks spent in endeavouring to get a position for him, he cannot get a position, nobody will have him. Nine hundred dollars a year is not sufficient for him with his wife and children, who sometimes are sick. He is sometimes sick too. All these things have to be taken into consideration. The minister has a good deal of courage; let him not be afraid to bring down proper estimates, because this is a department that should not be cut down 40 per cent, and it is not economy at all to economize at the veteran's expense. The people of Canada are well able to pay a proper debt of gratitude which they owe to the soldiers who went overseas for one, two, three, four or five years, and who, on their return to Canada, have technicalities and law dealt out to them, to deprive them of their rights, and who are done out of proper pensions and proper medical treatment by technicalities. They should have proper medical treatment

The criticism which

The various doctors were looking after these people. When they had a thousand patients it was absolutely necessary to have the medical attendance, but they would require the ordinary medical attendance if they had only fifteen-

Surely my hon. friend
wouM not claim for a minute that the doctors should be paid the same salary for looking after a small number of patients? Could they not be paid for part time?

That is not the question that the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), brought before the House at all. He said that the fee should be proportionate. My hon. friend is a medical doctor, and so is his deskmate (Mr. MacLaren), who are good friends of the soldiers and who both are returned soldiers. But I went into this matter last November With the various departments of Camp Hill hospital. I am interested in this matter as a citizen, and I wanted to find out exactly where Camp Hill hospital stood as regards the proportionate decrease in attendance of patients and everything else. They have their specialists who come certain days in the week. You cannot get a specialist to go to a hospital-I do not care if it is a soldiers' hospital or any other kind of a hospital-without paying his fee. They go on certain occasions and they receive the same fees. If there are ten patients in Camp Hill hospital now as compared with 1,000 patients three years ago, there cannot be the same proportionate decrease in expenditure.

Not the proportionate
decrease.

I appeal to my hon.
friends as men who know something about this, to be fair.
I agree that the proportionate decrease would not be as one thousand to ten, but the hon. member stated that you practically have to pay the same money to the doctors.
No.
He denies it now.

I am discussing a statement made by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), who ordinarily is a fair-minded man, a man for whom I have every respect. He stated, as I understood it
Supply-Re-establishment

and as, I think, the minister understood it when he replied, that the decrease should be proportionate.
He denied afterwards that he said that.

He said it. I will wager that his name will appear in Hansard as having said that very thing. It is just as well for us to consider everything in connection with this matter. Various hospitals have been closed down in this country and the decrease there, of course, is not proportionate to the decrease in the number of patients who may be in the district, because those patients will be sent to some other hospital. I appeal to my bon. friends who know something about this matter, that if there be ten, fifteen, or twenty patients in a hospital, outside of nursing care, you are not going to get doctors in this country for nothing. They may, of course, be part-time men. I know medical men who visit Camp Hill hospital at the present time to see friends, and who do that gratis, who charge no fees, who aire not connected with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment or the Pensions Commission in any way. At the same time, after some consideration of the matter, I submit that a proportionate decrease is absolutely impossible, because you must have the hospital, you must have the attendants in smaller numbers, you must have the doctors to look after the various cases. If there is a case of incipient insanity, you must bring in -a doctor who will be able to cope with the matter. If there is a case of tuberculosis amongst the ten patients that I have mentioned, you must bring in a doctor who is able to cope with a case of tuberculosis. If there is a case of kidney trouble and the department requires a certificate or description of the man's case, you must bring in a specialist in that disease. In that way I say that the hon. member for South Wellington is rather wrong in his analysis of the whole situation; that the decrease as regards the officials is not and cannot be proportionate to the decrease as regards the patients. I am one of those who think that, whatever amount of money is necessary to look after the unfortunate patients who are in our hospitals at the present time, it does not matter whether it is proportionate to the number of patients or not. The patients should have absolutely the same attention and care if there are only ten as if there were one thousand. I find fault sometimes with my hon. friends on the other side of the House, and I sometimes find fault with the Minister of Public Health and

the minister who looks after the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and pensions. I feel that hospitals in this country were closed dlown without justification, and that if there were fifteen or twenty patients to be treated in a district, the hospital should be kept open. When those men were asked to enlist in Canada, they were promised everything; they were promised that nothing that Canada could do for them would be too good. Nevertheless, I find some hon. gentlemen-I am glad to say there are not returned soldiers amongst them-on the other side of the House and sometimes on this side, Who complain about the amount of money which the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and the Pensions Commission are costing this country. Personally, while I feel that we must -act carefully and justify the various steps that we take, we must still continue for years to come to give our returned- soldiers, who happened to come back to this country in an unfortunate condition of health, the very best of -care that this country can give them. If we do that, the hon. member for South Wellington is far wrong in his suggestion that the number of officials who are treating those patients or the officials in connection with the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is over-proportioned to the number of patients Who are being treated.

I should like to say a few
words in reply to the hon. member, because the impression might be left from his remarks that the hon. member for South Wellington suggested not giving proper attention to the soldiers or the pensioners.
I did not say that.

Was that not what the
hon. member for South Wellington complained about, that they were not proportionate?

My hon. friend'complains
that it is impossible for them to be proportionate.
Yes.

They were nearly proportionate. In 1923, there were 3,744 patients with 3,524 of a staff. This year there are 3,444 patients with 3,094 of a staff. Roughly the decrease is proportionate. In fact, the decrease in the staff has been greater than the decrease in the number of patients.

My hon. friend does not
agree with his friend the hon. member for South Wellington.

I do not know exactly
what my hon. friend means by not agreeing with the hon. member for South Wellington.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The hon. member had
better stick to his own ideas.

I am pointing out that there is more or less of a proportionate decrease in the staff and the number of patients. I agree that you cannot make a cast iron rule in this case. I do not agree with my hon. friend when he says that ten or fifteen patients must receive the same care as 1,000 patients. That was the expression he used. As a matter of fact, when you get down to a low number of patients you naturally can put the doctors on part time and pay them according to the work they do. Certainly for 100 patients you should not have to pay for anything like the same amount of medical attention as you do for 1,000 men, and of course for 15 you would pay enormously less in proportion. You pay the medical men in proportion to the work they do, and as a matter of fact that is what the department has generally done. In my own city for example there was a medical officer doing work for the department. He was not giving full time and was receiving $200 a month a year or two ago. To-day he receives half that because the work has decreased. It is true doctors must be paid, but they are paid in proportion to
the work they do. Now, Mr. Chairman, I suggest to the minister that as it is 11.45 we adjourn. There is bound to be further discussion on this item and it would be well for the minister to report progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have no objection, but we have passed only one small item. I would suggest that we allow this item to carry, with the understanding that the discussion can be held later.

I do not want the minister to think that we are trying to obstruct; there will be :io obstruction at all. But hon. members wish to discuss this item further and I would suggest that he move the adjournment.
There are just one or two points on which I should like some information before we adjourn to-night. What institutions of the department are at present in operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: We have only two, Mowat in Kingston and the Central Alberta in Calgary. These are two exclusively tubercular institutions.
What about Tranquille?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It is not operated by the department. I take it that the hon. member is referring to institutions that are entirely-operated by the department, of which we have two.

I wish to know what institutions for treatment of tuberculosis are wholly under the control of the department, and the minister says there are two. At the. present time he is proposing to relieve himself of the Mowat memorial hospital.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Yes.
And to hand it over to the provincial authorities or some one else.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: To the owners; the hospital is under lease.

The point I want to make when the matter comes up for discussion again is that this is only shifting the responsibility in this matter. I will criticise the department in this respect, and at the same time I shall have some suggestions to offer as to how the department could carry its responsibility and still relieve itself of a good deal of its burden. At present, however, the minister says there are only two such institutions. Are there any tubercular cases in Gravenhurst?
Supply-Re-establishment

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: There are 32.

Can the minister
tell us how many ex-serviee men are in Gravenhurst not under the care of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have not the information.
Does the minister not know how many there are in that institution not receiving support from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I have no idea.

Does the minister
know there are nearly 30?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I do not know.
Are you paying for Canadian tubercular patients in the United States and England? The annual report says there are 95 such patients.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
We have tubercular
patients in the United States and in the British Isles, yes.

Will the minister have available, when next this matter comes up, information as to the number of the staff in the British Columbia unit-Unit J.-on part time as well as those on full time, including medical officers of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: The hon. member is referring to the number of officials and doctors?
The officials and doctors of the medical examination branch and the travelling boards.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to Vancouver?
No, I am referring to the whole province.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
We have in J. Unit 6
medical men on full time and six on part time. In Shaughnessy hospital we have three on full time and four on part time. In Victoria we have two medical representatives, one is on full time and one on part time; and in Kamloops we have one representative on part time. This makes a total for that unit of ten on full time and twelve on part time.

Has the minister any
information available for the year 1921 in regard to this particular matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
On January 1, 1922, in
that unit there were seventeen on full time and twenty on part time. I move, Mr. Chairman, that the committee rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Item 292 has been
agreed to. This item stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
With the permission of
the House I should like to move the following resolution:
That said bill be referred to a special committee of the members of this House, with instructions to send for persons, papers and records and to report from time to time.
